pitfalls: GFR and ACR results may be recorded on different dates and never brought together in one place → the calculator should pull the most recent value of each, regardless of date, and flag if either is more than 12 months old.
Staff may record the individual numeric results without translating them into the categorical grid → make the categorical output, not just the raw numbers, the audited item.
Patients under nephrology may have their classification documented only in hospital letters → check for this before counting as a gap in the GP record.
A single ACR result in category A2/A3 needs confirmation before acting on it clinically, per NICE → note this distinction in staff training so classification and clinical action are not conflated.
Improvement may fade if the calculator is not maintained after an EPR template change → confirm it remains functional at re-audit.
pearls: Recruit the practice's CKD lead nurse or clinical pharmacist to champion the automatic calculator.
Agree the calculator's exact grid values with NICE table 1 before building it, to avoid errors.
Use the same CKD register definition at re-audit for a fair comparison.
Report documentation rates at the QOF/long-term conditions meeting to keep this visible after the lead rotates.

pitfalls: Routine blood monitoring can be mistaken for the full annual risk review, when it only covers some of the required factors → keep the two as clearly separate template items.

Interacting medicines (for example, trimethoprim prescribed by an out-of-hours service) may not trigger an alert if prescribed outside the practice → include a manual interaction check as part of the annual review.
Alcohol intake may be under-reported → use a standard, non-judgemental question as part of the review.
Shared care responsibilities between specialist and GP may be unclear for who leads the annual risk review → confirm this explicitly in the shared care agreement before cycle 1.
Improvement may fade if the annual review template is not linked to a recall system → build in an automatic annual reminder.
pearls: Recruit the practice's clinical pharmacist to lead the annual risk review process.
Agree with the rheumatology or gastroenterology shared care team which factors and thresholds to use before cycle 1.
Use the same DMARD register definitions at re-audit for a fair comparison.
Report annual review completion at the medicines optimisation meeting to sustain the process after staff rotate.

pitfalls: Ambulance and ED clocks are not synchronised → agree a single timestamp source before cycle 1
Small numbers on quiet shifts hide the true delay → sample across day, evening and night shifts
Definition of 'handover accepted' drifts between cycles → lock the definition (first ED clinician contact) in writing with the ambulance trust liaison
Ambulance and nursing staff see this as blame-shifting → present it jointly as a shared flow problem, not a performance league table
Gains fade once the streaming nurse post is not backfilled on leave → build it into the establishment, not a rota extra
pearls: Recruit the ambulance trust liaison officer as a co-presenter before cycle 1
Agree the timestamp definitions with both organisations in writing before data collection starts
Display live handover times on the department screen so staff see the effect of the change in real time
Link the audit to the trust's existing corridor-care or ambulance-queue safety huddle so it does not need a new meeting

pitfalls: Radio recordings are hard to retrieve after a few days → agree a retrieval process with the ambulance trust before cycle 1
Small sample if trauma calls are infrequent → extend the collection window to 6 weeks in a lower-volume unit
Definitions of 'given' vary between reviewers → agree a one-page scoring key before starting
Ambulance crews may feel audited without being consulted → involve the trust's trauma desk lead in designing the proforma
Improvement fades once new crews rotate in → add ATMIST training to ambulance trust induction
pearls: Get sign-off from the trauma network's clinical lead before starting, since the change affects the ambulance trust too
Use existing trauma network governance meetings to close the loop rather than creating a new forum
Pilot the ATMIST proforma on one ambulance station before a wider rollout
Keep the same reviewer for both cycles to reduce scoring drift

pitfalls: Readiness is hard to verify retrospectively → use direct observation for at least half the sample
Staff may complete the checklist after the event to look compliant → timestamp the checklist electronically
Small numbers if major trauma calls are rare → extend the collection window
Rota gaps mean no consultant TTL is available out of hours → escalate staffing gaps found by the audit to rota planning
Improvement fades once the tabard goes missing → keep a spare stock in the resus room
pearls: Recruit the trauma coordinator to help design and pilot the checklist
Agree with nursing and ED consultant leads before cycle 1 who owns team readiness
Use the trauma governance meeting, which already exists, to close the loop
Keep the audit tool the same across cycles so the readiness rate is directly comparable

pitfalls: 999 call time and drug administration time are recorded on different systems → agree the linkage method with the ambulance trust before cycle 1
Small numbers because pre-hospital RSI is rare → pool data across a longer period or across the regional network
Case-mix varies (rural versus urban scenes) → record scene location type to interpret outliers
Crews may feel individually blamed for system delays → present aggregated, anonymised timelines only
Improvement is not sustained after staff turnover on the critical care desk → build the RSI-time review into the desk's standard handover
pearls: Agree data-sharing with the ambulance/critical care service before starting, since most of the data sits outside the hospital
Recruit the regional trauma network's pre-hospital lead as co-owner of the audit
Use the existing trauma governance meeting to close the loop
Keep case numbers pooled across the network if a single trust's volume is too small to interpret alone

pitfalls: Free-text fluid records make coding inconsistent → agree a coding key with the ambulance trust before cycle 1
Blood component availability varies by crew type, confounding comparisons → record crew type for every case
Small numbers if pre-hospital blood is well established locally → pool across the network
Crews may see this as second-guessing a scene decision → frame feedback as system learning, not individual performance
Gains fade if new crews are not told about the change → add to annual mandatory pre-hospital training
pearls: Involve the ambulance trust's clinical governance lead from the start
Use the trauma network's existing pre-hospital blood programme meeting to close the loop
Keep the same fluid-choice coding key for both cycles
Share results with crews as a learning bulletin, not a performance table

pitfalls: Time of injury is often uncertain → exclude or flag cases with an estimated rather than witnessed injury time
Ambulance and ED records are on separate systems → agree a single audit form covering both before cycle 1
Small numbers in a district general hospital → extend the collection period to 6-12 months
Clinicians may worry about giving TXA before imaging excludes a contraindication → reinforce the NICE wording ('before imaging') in training
Gains fade if the prompt is switched off during a system upgrade → check it after any EPR update
pearls: Agree with the ambulance trust which record system will supply the injury-time and TXA-time fields before starting
Recruit a trauma nurse coordinator to flag eligible cases prospectively as a data-collection aid
Present pooled ambulance and hospital data together so both services see the whole pathway
Keep the same eligibility criteria (GCS ≤12, no extracranial bleeding) across cycles

pitfalls: Ambulance and hospital notes may be scored differently by different reviewers → use one trained reviewer for the whole audit
Paediatric cases are infrequent, giving small numbers → extend the sampling period for the under-5 subgroup
Ambulance crews may feel individually singled out → report results in aggregate only
Definitions of 'correct version' can be disputed at the 5-year-old boundary → agree the cut-off with the ambulance trust in advance
Improvement is not sustained after a change of electronic patient record supplier → re-check the prompt after any system change
pearls: Agree access to ambulance patient report forms with the ambulance trust's information governance team before starting
Involve the ambulance trust's clinical education lead in interpreting results
Use existing joint governance meetings rather than creating a new one
Keep the same scoring key across both cycles

pitfalls: Safeguarding flags on ambulance forms are often free text and easy to miss at triage → make the field mandatory rather than free text
Small numbers given expected low case volume → extend the collection period to 6 months
Information governance restrictions on accessing ambulance safeguarding data → agree data-sharing with the ambulance trust's safeguarding lead first
Staff may under-report to avoid extra paperwork → make the field quick (drop-down, not free text)
Loop closure stalls if the safeguarding committee meets infrequently → agree a fixed re-audit slot on the agenda in advance
pearls: Involve both trusts' safeguarding leads from the outset, since this is a cross-organisational pathway
Use the existing safeguarding committee to close the loop rather than a new meeting
Keep the case definition (types of flag counted) identical across cycles
Share anonymised case learning, not identifiable feedback, with individual crews

pitfalls: Bed availability on the stroke unit may block direct conveyance regardless of the pathway → record bed availability as a separate field
Small numbers in a unit without a hyperacute stroke service → adjust the pathway definition to the local model of care
FAST-positive pre-alerts may be over- or under-called → cross check against the final stroke/TIA/stroke-mimic diagnosis
ED staff may resist bypassing initial ED assessment → involve ED consultants in agreeing exceptions (e.g. unstable airway) in advance
Gains fade if the stroke unit's bed-holding process is not maintained → review bed-holding capacity at the re-audit
pearls: Agree the direct-conveyance protocol jointly with ambulance, ED and stroke medicine before cycle 1
Use the stroke operational delivery network meeting, which already exists, to close the loop
Track bed availability as a confounder so failures to bypass are not all attributed to the pathway
Keep the FAST-positive definition identical across both cycles

pitfalls: Patients who self-medicate with aspirin before the ambulance arrives may be miscounted → record 'already taken' as a separate category
Small numbers of pre-hospital STEMI diagnoses in a smaller ambulance sector → pool data across the cardiac network
Allergy documentation is sometimes missing rather than a true contraindication → distinguish 'documented allergy' from 'not recorded'
Crews may feel blamed for a system-level cath lab bottleneck → keep the audit focused on the aspirin step only
Gains fade if the mandatory field is removed in a system update → recheck after any ambulance ePR change
pearls: Agree data access with the ambulance trust's cardiac clinical lead before starting
Use the cardiac network's existing primary PCI governance meeting to close the loop
Keep the STEMI diagnosis definition (ambulance 12-lead ECG criteria) identical across cycles
Share results as a learning bulletin for crews, not a named performance table

pitfalls: Pulse oximetry can be unreliable in a cold, shut-down post-arrest patient → record whether the SpO2 reading was judged reliable
Small numbers given expected low ROSC volume → extend the collection period or pool with a neighbouring ambulance sector
Crews may keep FiO2 high out of caution → reinforce the harm of hyperoxaemia in training, not just hypoxaemia
Definitions of 'reliable SpO2' vary → agree a working definition with the ambulance trust before cycle 1
Gains fade without refresher training after the initial rollout → add to the annual post-resuscitation care update
pearls: Link the audit to the trust's existing out-of-hospital cardiac arrest outcomes review meeting
Recruit a resuscitation officer from both the ambulance trust and the ED as joint audit leads
Keep the SpO2 target and 'reliable reading' definitions identical for both cycles
Feed results back through the ambulance trust's cardiac arrest governance process, which already exists

pitfalls: Presumed cardiac cause is a judgement call and can be coded inconsistently → agree the coding criteria with ambulance clinicians before cycle 1
Rural areas may have long transfer times to the PCI centre → record transfer distance as a confounder
Small numbers given expected low ROSC volume → pool data across the network if a single ambulance sector is too small
Onward inter-hospital transfers add delay and risk if the algorithm is not followed → track onward transfers as a secondary outcome
Improvement is not sustained if the algorithm is not built into ambulance dispatch software → make it a system default rather than a memory-based decision
pearls: Agree the destination algorithm jointly between the ambulance trust and the cardiac network before starting
Use the existing out-of-hospital cardiac arrest outcomes governance meeting to close the loop
Keep the 'presumed cardiac cause' definition identical across both cycles
Track time from ROSC to cath lab as well as destination choice, since it is the outcome that matters clinically

pitfalls: Continuous core temperature monitoring devices are not always available → record the monitoring method used (core probe, bladder, tympanic)
Small numbers because comatose ROSC admissions are infrequent → extend the collection period to 6-12 months
Staff may treat fever reactively rather than proactively → make the order set nurse-initiated so no medical review delay is needed
Definitions of 'active prevention' vary between units → agree what counts (paracetamol, cooling blanket, ice packs) before cycle 1
Gains fade after critical care nursing rotation → include in critical care induction training
pearls: Recruit the critical care outreach or resuscitation officer team to help identify eligible cases prospectively
Use an existing critical care mortality and morbidity or resuscitation governance meeting to close the loop
Keep the 37.7°C threshold and monitoring definitions identical across cycles
Track antipyretic administration alongside temperature trend, not temperature alone

pitfalls: Non-conveyed falls attendances are not always well documented → agree a minimum dataset with the ambulance trust before cycle 1
Falls services vary in how they accept ambulance referrals → confirm the referral route works before auditing uptake
Small numbers if 'not conveyed' coding is inconsistent → review ambulance coding practice first
Ambulance crews under time pressure may skip the referral step → make it a single click in the ePR rather than a phone call
Gains fade if the falls service cannot cope with increased referrals → agree capacity with the falls service before scaling up
pearls: Involve the community falls service lead and the ambulance trust's falls lead together from the start
Use the trust's existing falls prevention steering group to close the loop
Keep the NG249 referral criteria identical across both cycles
Track whether referrals are actually acted on by the falls service, not just made

pitfalls: Patients may not know or disclose that a medicine is time-critical → use the UKCPA poster to prompt disclosure
Triage staff may not recognise all time-critical drug classes → use the MISSED mnemonic (movement, immunomodulators, sugar, steroids, epilepsy, DOACs) in training
Small numbers if flagging is inconsistent → audit the flagging rate itself as a secondary measure
ED pharmacy may not have 24/7 cover → record time of day to see if out-of-hours delays predominate
Improvement fades once the initial safety flash awareness fades → repeat the poster and training at 6-monthly intervals
pearls: Display the RCEM/UKCPA poster at triage before starting data collection
Recruit the ED pharmacist as a co-lead, since medicines availability is part of the standard
Use the trust medication safety group, which already exists, to close the loop
Keep the same list of time-critical drug classes (the MISSED categories) across both cycles

pitfalls: Adrenal crisis presentations are non-specific and easily missed → use the RCEM safety flash's red-flag list (nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain, confusion, syncope, unexplained fever, long-lie) as the case-finding filter
Small numbers given expected low volume → extend the collection period to 12 months if needed
Steroid cards are not always carried → also check EPR medication history and GP summary care record
Hydrocortisone may not be immediately available on the resus trolley → confirm stock location with pharmacy before cycle 1
Gains fade once the safety flash is no longer fresh in staff minds → repeat awareness training at 6-monthly intervals
pearls: Display the NHS Steroid Emergency Card image at triage as a visual prompt
Recruit an ED pharmacist to confirm hydrocortisone stocking before starting
Use the ED patient safety meeting, which already exists, to close the loop
Keep the case-finding red-flag list identical across both cycles

pitfalls: High-risk criteria may not be explicitly documented by ambulance crews → agree a checklist with the ambulance trust before cycle 1
Small numbers given expected low paediatric sepsis volume → pool across a longer period or with a neighbouring trust
Pre-alert calls may mention 'unwell child' without naming sepsis specifically → record whether the word 'sepsis' or 'high risk' was used
Ambulance crews may feel audited without being consulted → involve the paediatric-trained ambulance clinical lead in the design
Gains fade once the decision-support prompt is switched off in an update → recheck after any ambulance system change
pearls: Link the audit to the existing paediatric sepsis quality improvement work already running in the ED
Recruit a paediatric emergency nurse and the ambulance trust's paediatric lead as joint owners
Use the paediatric emergency governance meeting to close the loop
Track time to antibiotics as the outcome that ultimately matters, alongside the process measure of pre-alerting

pitfalls: Corridor-care time is not always logged separately from cubicle time → agree a location-logging method before cycle 1
Staff may under-document during periods of extreme pressure, the exact time this audit targets → use direct spot-checks as well as retrospective chart review
Numbers vary hugely by day-of-week surge → sample across several different pressure levels
Staff may see this as adding more paperwork during an already unsafe situation → pair the audit with the safety-nurse role, not extra forms
Improvement is not sustained if the role is dropped once escalation pressure eases → keep it as a standing response to a defined occupancy trigger
pearls: Agree with senior nursing and medical leads what counts as 'corridor care' before starting
Use the trust's existing overcrowding/escalation policy meeting to close the loop
Track NEWS2 escalation, not just observation frequency, as the outcome that matters
Keep the same location-logging method for both cycles

pitfalls: CFS scoring needs a collateral history, which is not always available at triage → allow a 'provisional score, confirm later' option
Staff may not be trained in CFS scoring → provide a laminated CFS reference card at every triage desk
Small numbers if attendance data is not filtered correctly by age → double-check the age filter before sampling
Recording a score without acting on it (no referral) undermines the point → audit the referral step as well as the recording step
Gains fade after new starters join triage → add CFS training to ED induction
pearls: Involve the frailty/geriatric medicine team in designing the referral trigger before cycle 1
Use existing frailty service governance meetings to close the loop
Keep the referral threshold (CFS ≥5) identical across both cycles
Display CFS reference cards at every triage station, not just centrally

pitfalls: Point-of-care and laboratory potassium results may be recorded on different systems → agree a single result-timestamp source before cycle 1
Small numbers given expected low volume of severe hyperkalaemia → extend the collection period to 6-12 months
ECG-change cases without an extreme potassium value are easy to miss in a lab-based search → also screen ED ECGs reported as hyperkalaemic pattern
Nursing may wait for medical review before giving calcium → confirm local policy allows nurse-initiated calcium via a patient group direction or protocol
Gains fade if the automatic order set is switched off in a system update → recheck after any EPR change
pearls: Agree the case-finding method (lab result search plus ECG report search) with the laboratory and ED IT teams before starting
Recruit an ED pharmacist to help design the order set
Use the ED patient safety meeting, which already exists, to close the loop
Keep the 6.5 mmol/L and 15-minute definitions identical across both cycles

pitfalls: Mild or vague presentations (headache, flu-like symptoms) may not trigger suspicion → add a seasonal awareness campaign (winter heating season) alongside the audit
Small numbers given expected low local volume → extend the collection period to 12 months
Co-oximetry may not be available on every blood gas analyser → confirm equipment availability before cycle 1
Household/multiple casualties may not all be flagged to the same audit → cross-check ambulance dispatch data for clustered presentations
Gains fade outside the winter season when suspicion is lower → repeat awareness training before each heating season
pearls: Recruit ED toxicology/poisons information (TOXBASE) contacts as a resource, not a data source, when designing the order set
Use the ED patient safety meeting to close the loop
Keep the same case-finding method (clerking note search for 'carbon monoxide' or 'CO poisoning') across both cycles
Coordinate with the fire and rescue service so household safety checks follow confirmed cases

pitfalls: Families may already own auto-injectors, making 'supplied' an incomplete measure → record 'supplied or confirmed in-date and carried' as the combined pass criterion
Written action plans are sometimes given verbally only → audit for a physical or electronic copy actually handed over, not just advice given
Small numbers if paediatric anaphylaxis presentations are infrequent → extend the collection period to 6 months
Stock shortages of auto-injector trainer devices can limit training → confirm trainer-device stock with pharmacy before cycle 1
Gains fade if new staff are not shown the mandatory bundle → add to paediatric ED induction
pearls: Recruit the paediatric allergy service to help design the action-plan template
Use the paediatric emergency governance meeting to close the loop
Keep the discharge bundle definition identical across both cycles
Stock auto-injectors and action plans directly in paediatric bays to remove a barrier to completion

pitfalls: Pain scores are not always recorded at triage → include 'no pain score recorded' as its own category rather than excluding these patients
NSAID contraindications (renal impairment, GI bleed history) may not be checked before an audit reviewer assumes non-compliance → record contraindications explicitly
Small numbers in a lower-volume unit → extend the collection period to 6 weeks
Nursing staff may be reluctant to give analgesia before a doctor review → confirm the patient group direction is signed off by the relevant clinical governance committee before cycle 1
Gains fade if the patient group direction is not refreshed on renewal → set a renewal reminder alongside the re-audit date
pearls: Agree the patient group direction with pharmacy and medical leadership before starting
Recruit a triage nurse champion to help embed the new prompt
Use the ED pain management meeting, which already exists for other analgesia audits, to close the loop
Keep the pain-score threshold and analgesia options identical across both cycles

pitfalls: Observations may be recorded as part of routine hourly obs rather than a specific post-opioid check, making them hard to attribute → record the nearest observation time relative to the dose, not just whether one exists in the hour
Sedation scoring tools vary between departments → agree a single sedation scale before cycle 1
Small numbers on quieter shifts → sample across different times of day
Nursing staff already stretched may see this as extra burden → pair with the automatic EPMA task rather than a manual checklist
Gains fade if the EPMA task is removed in an update → recheck after any system change
pearls: Agree the sedation scoring tool with anaesthetics/critical care outreach before starting, so it is consistent across the hospital
Recruit an ED pharmacist to help design the EPMA task
Use the ED patient safety meeting to close the loop
Keep the 30-minute window and sedation scale identical across both cycles

pitfalls: Verbal advice may be given but not documented → audit only what is written in the record, and note this limitation when presenting results
Leaflet availability may run out during busy shifts → confirm stock levels with the ED matron before cycle 1
Small numbers if sepsis screening is not consistently coded → cross-check against the sepsis screening tool completion rate
Staff may see this as an extra step in an already complex pathway → automate the print rather than relying on staff to remember
Gains fade if the automatic print is switched off in a system change → recheck after any EPR update
pearls: Use the existing sepsis steering group to design and own the leaflet trigger
Recruit an ED nurse educator to reinforce safety-netting messaging at induction
Use the ED patient safety meeting, which already exists for other sepsis audits, to close the loop
Keep the definition of 'sepsis screen performed' identical across both cycles

pitfalls: Undiagnosed COPD patients may not be flagged → include 'newly suspected' cases identified from smoking history and examination, not only coded diagnoses
Staff may prescribe 94-98% by habit → make the correct range the system default rather than relying on memory
Small numbers on quieter shifts → sample across a longer period if COPD presentations are infrequent
Definitions of 'at risk of hypercapnia' can be disputed → agree the criteria (known COPD, previous NIV, known CO2 retention) before cycle 1
Gains fade if the default is changed in a system update → recheck after any EPR change
pearls: Involve the respiratory team in agreeing the target-range default and override reasons
Recruit an ED pharmacist to help build the mandatory field
Use joint ED-respiratory governance to close the loop
Keep the 88-92% threshold and 'at risk' definition identical across both cycles

pitfalls: Weekend and overnight presentations are the most likely to breach 24 hours → analyse weekday versus weekend/overnight separately
Haemodynamically unstable patients go straight to theatre and should be analysed separately, not counted as a breach → exclude or flag them
Small numbers in a unit with a low volume of early pregnancy attendances → extend the collection period to 6 weeks
Referral may be made but the appointment not actually booked → audit the actual scan/review time, not just referral completion
Gains fade if weekend gynaecology cover is not sustained → confirm the out-of-hours pathway is resourced before scaling up
pearls: Agree the out-of-hours pathway with gynaecology before starting data collection
Recruit the early pregnancy assessment unit lead as a co-owner of the audit
Use the joint ED-gynaecology governance meeting to close the loop
Keep the referral criteria and 24-hour definition identical across both cycles

pitfalls: Suspicion is not always explicitly time-stamped in free-text notes → train staff to write the time of suspicion as a discrete entry
Small numbers given the expected low volume of this presentation → collect over 6-12 months or pool across a vascular network
Switchboard/bleep delays may be outside ED control → record whether the delay was in ED referral or in reaching the vascular team
Anticoagulation may be delayed while awaiting vascular advice → audit this as a secondary process measure
Gains fade if the one-click referral button is removed in an EPR update → recheck after any system change
pearls: Agree the case-finding method (clerking note text search for limb ischaemia symptoms) with ED and vascular leads before starting
Recruit the vascular surgery on-call rota lead as a co-owner of the audit
Use the joint ED-vascular governance meeting to close the loop
Keep the 30-minute definition and referral method identical across both cycles

pitfalls: Tracking system timestamps can be inaccurate if staff log in retrospectively → spot-check a sample against direct observation
Occupancy pressure is the main driver of delay and is outside the audit's control → record occupancy as a confounder, not an excuse to exclude cases
Small numbers on quiet shifts → sample across day, evening and night shifts
Staff may feel individually blamed for system-level overcrowding → present results as a department-level flow measure, not a named performance table
Gains fade once escalation fatigue sets in during sustained high occupancy → review escalation triggers at the re-audit
pearls: Agree the triage-category definitions with the ED triage lead before starting
Use the department's existing flow/safety huddle to close the loop
Keep the 10-minute definition and category 2 criteria identical across both cycles
Track occupancy alongside compliance so the effect of flow pressure is visible, not hidden

pitfalls: New AF is sometimes coded under a general 'palpitations' diagnosis → search discharge diagnoses broadly, not just the exact AF code
Score components (hypertension, diabetes, vascular disease history) may be incompletely documented → record 'unable to calculate, missing data' as its own category
Small numbers in a lower-volume unit → extend the collection period to 6 weeks
Clinicians may defer the decision to the GP without a formal score → count 'deferred with reason' as a partial pass only if the score itself is still documented
Gains fade if the mandatory field is bypassed by overriding it → monitor override rates at the re-audit
pearls: Agree the discharge coding search terms with the ED coding/informatics team before starting
Recruit a cardiology liaison clinician to help design the mandatory field and anticoagulation guidance
Use the joint ED-cardiology governance meeting to close the loop
Keep the CHA2DS2-VASc calculation method and pass definition identical across both cycles

pitfalls: Non-conveyed episodes are not always separately coded from other 'not conveyed' outcomes → agree a coding filter with the ambulance trust before cycle 1
Care and safety plans may exist in mental health records the ambulance crew cannot access in real time → record whether the crew had access to the plan, not just whether one existed
Small numbers given how this presentation is coded → extend the collection period to 6 months
Crews may under-document sensitive conversations → keep the audit tool short and focused on the specific NG225 items
Gains fade if the crisis team referral route is not resourced → confirm capacity with the crisis team before scaling up
pearls: Involve the ambulance trust's mental health lead and the local crisis team from the start
Use an existing joint mental health/ambulance governance meeting to close the loop
Keep the coding filter for 'self-harm, not conveyed' identical across both cycles
Track whether alternative services were actually accessed, not just discussed, as a secondary outcome

pitfalls: Very low case numbers make single-trust audit under-powered → pool data across the regional trauma network
Retrospective documentation may under-record the clinical picture at the time of decision → use direct crew debrief where possible, in addition to the written record
Post-decompression observation for recurrence is a separate but related safety step → record this alongside indication appropriateness
Crews may feel individually scrutinised for a rare, high-stakes decision → present findings in aggregate, with a focus on system learning
Gains fade without regular case-based teaching → use real (anonymised) cases in the annual training update
pearls: Agree with the regional trauma network's pre-hospital lead to pool data across the network before starting
Recruit a HEMS/critical care paramedic clinical lead as co-owner of the audit
Use the trauma governance meeting, which already exists, to close the loop
Keep the indication definitions (haemodynamic instability, severe respiratory compromise) identical across both cycles

pitfalls: Small numbers given expected low volume of warfarin-associated intracranial haemorrhage → extend the collection period to 12 months
PCC may be delayed by blood bank turnaround time rather than a clinical decision delay → record the time PCC was requested as well as when it was given
INR results may lag behind the clinical decision to reverse → do not delay treatment purely for INR confirmation, in line with the guideline's intent, and audit accordingly
DOAC-treated patients need a different reversal agent and should not be mixed into this sample → keep the two anticoagulant types in separate audits
Gains fade if the order set is switched off in an EPR update → recheck after any system change
pearls: Agree the order set design with haematology and pharmacy before starting
Recruit an ED pharmacist to identify eligible cases prospectively as a data-collection aid
Use the ED-haematology joint governance meeting, which already exists, to close the loop
Keep the same reversal-timing definition (from CT report to administration) across both cycles

pitfalls: Rural geography may mean bypass is not always feasible within the 120-minute window → record travel time and distance as confounders
Small numbers in a smaller ambulance sector → pool data across the cardiac network
Ambulance ECG transmission failures can force a default to the nearest ED → record technical failures as a separate reason category
Crews may default to the nearest ED out of habit → reinforce the bypass threshold in annual cardiac pathway training
Gains fade if cath lab activation from the ambulance ECG is not reliably actioned → audit cath lab response time alongside conveyance decision
pearls: Agree the bypass-distance threshold jointly with the ambulance trust and cardiac network before starting
Use the existing primary PCI governance meeting to close the loop
Keep the 12-hour symptom-onset window and destination definitions identical across both cycles
Track call-to-balloon time as the ultimate outcome, alongside the process measure of direct conveyance

pitfalls: Traffic light features may be assessed inconsistently by non-paediatric-trained crews → provide a laminated traffic-light reference card on every vehicle
Small numbers given expected low volume of red-flag paediatric fever calls → extend the collection period to 12 months
Parents may decline conveyance despite advice → record 'declined against advice' as its own category, not a system failure
Ambulance and hospital records may use different fever assessment tools → agree a shared traffic-light tool with the paediatric department
Gains fade without refresher training → add to the ambulance trust's annual paediatric update
pearls: Agree the traffic-light assessment tool jointly with the paediatric emergency department before starting
Recruit the ambulance trust's paediatric clinical lead as a co-owner of the audit
Use the paediatric emergency governance meeting, which already exists, to close the loop
Keep the 'red feature' definition identical to the one used in the ED for continuity across the pathway

pitfalls: Capillary glucose may be checked but not documented in the neurological assessment section → search the whole ambulance record, not just the stroke-specific field
FAST scoring can be inconsistently applied by less experienced crews → provide a laminated FAST reference card on every vehicle
Small numbers if stroke-call coding is inconsistent → cross-check against the stroke pre-alert log as well as the neurological assessment field
Crews under time pressure may prioritise conveyance speed over full documentation → keep the mandatory fields quick (tick-box, not free text)
Gains fade without refresher training → add to the ambulance trust's annual stroke pathway update
pearls: Agree the mandatory field design with the ambulance trust's stroke clinical lead before starting
Use the stroke operational delivery network meeting, which already exists, to close the loop
Keep the FAST tool and glucose threshold definitions identical across both cycles
Track pre-alert accuracy (stroke mimics versus confirmed stroke) as a secondary measure of the pathway's overall quality

pitfalls: Anticoagulant use may not be reliably known at first assessment → cross-check with the GP summary care record and pharmacy medicines reconciliation
Small numbers given expected low volume of anticoagulated major trauma → extend the collection period to 12 months
Out-of-hours haematology advice may be by telephone and not always documented → agree a documentation standard for telephone advice before cycle 1

Reversal may be started before haematology is reached in a genuine emergency, which is appropriate → audit for a subsequent haematology discussion, not necessarily a prior one, in the most urgent cases
Gains fade if the mandatory field is not maintained after an EPR update → recheck after any system change
pearls: Agree the reversal pathway and documentation standard with haematology before starting
Recruit the trauma coordinator to flag eligible cases prospectively
Use the joint trauma-haematology governance meeting to close the loop
Keep the definitions of 'active or suspected bleeding' and 'reversal indicated' identical across both cycles

pitfalls: Pain scores are not always recorded consistently by all triage staff → audit the recording rate itself as a secondary measure
Nurse-initiated analgesia protocols need pharmacy and governance sign-off before use → secure this before cycle 1
Small numbers on quieter shifts → sample across different shift types
Some patients decline analgesia or have a contraindication, which should not count as a breach → record these separately, not as failures
Gains fade if the protocol lapses on renewal → set a renewal reminder alongside the re-audit date
pearls: Agree the nurse-initiated analgesia protocol with pharmacy and medical leadership before starting
Recruit a triage nurse champion to help embed the change
Use the ED pain management meeting, which already exists for other analgesia audits, to close the loop
Keep the pain-score threshold (≥7) and time window identical across both cycles

pitfalls: Responsibility for observations during a handover delay can be unclear between ambulance and ED staff → agree ownership explicitly before cycle 1
Small numbers if 60-minute-plus delays are rare (a good sign operationally, but limits audit power) → extend the collection period
Ambulance staff may be tied up with other calls during a queue → record which service (ambulance or ED) took each observation
Staff may see this as adding a role during an already unsafe situation → frame it as protecting patients, not adding paperwork
Gains fade once escalation pressure passes and the role is dropped informally → tie the role to a defined occupancy/queue-length trigger, not to memory
pearls: Use the trust's existing ambulance handover delay escalation policy meeting to close the loop
Recruit both an ED matron and an ambulance operations manager as joint audit owners
Keep the 60-minute delay threshold and 30-minute observation interval identical across both cycles
Track NEWS2 escalation events as the safety outcome that matters most, not just the observation count

pitfalls: Paper CTG annotations are often illegible or missing a time → agree a single place (trace margin or e-record) and a minimum data set with the labour ward before cycle 1
Small numbers if the unit has few continuous-CTG labours in the sample window → extend the collection period rather than lowering the sample
Staff may see the fresh-eyes prompt as another tick-box → involve labour ward coordinators in designing the prompt and explain the Each Baby Counts rationale
Definition of 'in-person' review may be interpreted loosely (a verbal comment vs a documented review) → fix the definition and a single documentation location before data collection starts
Gains fade once the audit team rotates → make the fresh-eyes field mandatory in the EPR build rather than relying on a poster reminder
pearls: Recruit a labour ward co-ordinator and a supervisor of midwives/PMA as co-investigators so the change has authority on the ward
Agree the exact fresh-eyes documentation field and audit definition with labour ward before cycle 1 starts
Time the audit to include day and night shifts, as fresh-eyes reviews are more often missed at night
Share individual near-miss examples (anonymised) at the labour ward forum to build buy-in before the second cycle
Keep the re-audit sample the same size and season to allow fair comparison

pitfalls: Paper partograms with gaps in recording → exclude labours with more than 20% missing entries and note the exclusion rate
Busy labour ward staffing may make 15-minute auscultation genuinely difficult → review staffing ratios alongside the audit, not instead of the process change
Definition of 'established first stage' varies between recorders → agree the definition (4 cm plus regular contractions) with the labour ward before data collection
One midwife's caseload dominating the sample → sample across shifts and midwives
Improvement fading after the audit team moves on → make the electronic timer the permanent default rather than a temporary poster
pearls: Recruit a practice development midwife to co-lead so the change is owned by the ward, not just the audit team
Pilot the electronic timer on one bay before full roll-out to iron out false alarms
Use real (anonymised) examples of delayed auscultation from incident reports to explain the 'why' at launch
Cross-reference with the labour ward's Each Baby Counts and MBRRACE-UK action plan so this audit is not seen as a duplicate task
Feed results back to individual midwives confidentially as well as to the team, to support learning

pitfalls: Ambiguity about the exact moment second stage starts → use the documented time of full dilatation or bearing-down urge as the trigger, agreed in advance
Very short second stages give few data points → record the number of auscultations expected as well as achieved
Staff may confuse this with the separate first-stage 15-minute standard → make the EPR mode change explicit and visible
Retrospective note review may miss verbal-only auscultations → accept only documented entries as per protocol
Losing momentum after go-live → include the second-stage timer in new starter induction
pearls: Pair this audit with the first-stage auscultation audit so both cycles share the same data collection visit
Get labour ward coordinator sign-off on the definition of second stage onset before starting
Use huddle boards to display real-time compliance during the embedding phase
Link learning to the unit's Each Baby Counts action plan
Keep sample size and season consistent at re-audit

pitfalls: Bishop score sometimes recorded narratively rather than as a number → accept only a numeric or component score as compliant
CTG performed but not formally reported before induction starts → require a documented category (normal/suspicious/pathological), not just a trace reference
Staff shortages leading to skipped pre-induction CTG on busy days → escalate persistent gaps to the labour ward matron
Retrospective note-finding may undercount compliance if records are split between paper and EPR → check both systems for each case
Definition drift between cycles (e.g. accepting an antenatal CTG from earlier in the day as 'pre-induction') → fix the definition (within 4 hours of starting) before cycle 1
pearls: Involve the induction ward coordinator in designing the proforma change
Pilot the new proforma for two weeks and fix obvious problems before the full re-audit
Use real anonymised delayed-recognition cases to make the case for the change at launch
Keep the same definition of 'before induction started' across both cycles
Feed back individual near-misses privately as well as team results

pitfalls: Legacy local practice (e.g. syntometrine as default) may persist after guidance changes → communicate the 2023 update explicitly to all grades of staff
Documentation of exact time relative to cord clamping is often absent → add a simple tick box rather than relying on free text
Small numbers if the maternity unit has a low birth rate → extend the collection period
Staff may conflate this with the caesarean carbetocin standard → make clear this audit is for vaginal births only
Improvement fading if the old pre-printed chart re-enters stock → destroy old stock once the new chart is live
pearls: Involve the labour ward pharmacist in redesigning the drug chart
Brief anaesthetic and obstetric staff as well as midwives, since doctors sometimes give the third-stage drug at instrumental births
Use a short teaching huddle to explain the rationale for the 2023 change (reduced side-effect burden with single-agent oxytocin where appropriate)
Display current compliance on the labour ward safety board
Keep the same definition of 'active management' between cycles

pitfalls: PPH events are relatively infrequent → extend the collection window to 6 months to reach an adequate sample
Emergency documentation is often incomplete under pressure → use a structured PPH proforma with timed boxes rather than free text
Staff may not know the correct infusion time (10 minutes, not a rapid push) → include this explicitly in PPH drills
Ambiguity about what counts as 'continuing' haemorrhage → define as bleeding continuing after the first uterotonic dose, agreed with the labour ward before cycle 1
Fading compliance once the initial drill enthusiasm passes → repeat PPH simulation drills quarterly with tranexamic acid timing as a scored item
pearls: Link this audit to the unit's regular PPH simulation training programme
Involve the obstetric anaesthetist and transfusion practitioner as co-investigators
Use the maternity haemorrhage box contents check as a natural trigger to review the drug card design
Present near-miss and good-practice cases anonymously at multidisciplinary training
Keep the same PPH volume threshold and definition of 'continuing' bleeding at re-audit

pitfalls: Cord clamping time is often estimated rather than timed → provide a wall clock or timer visible to the person clamping the cord
Staff may confuse this with the preterm cord-clamping standard → make clear in training that this audit covers term active-managed births
Retrospective note review may find blank fields rather than wrong values → record 'not documented' as a distinct category, not a fail by default, to identify where the gap is
Genuine clinical reasons for early clamping (cord integrity concern, poor condition at birth) must not be miscounted as non-compliance → capture the documented reason
Fading compliance after go-live → include the field in the maternity dashboard so gaps are visible weekly
pearls: Use a simple wall-mounted timer or the delivery room clock as a low-cost prompt
Recruit maternity support workers to help time and record cord clamping during the collection period
Link this audit with training on delayed cord clamping benefits for haemoglobin and iron stores
Present compliance trends, not just a single snapshot, to the labour ward forum
Keep the same window definition (1-5 minutes) and exclusions at re-audit

pitfalls: Skin-to-skin start/stop times are rarely documented precisely → accept nearest 5-minute estimates and note this limitation
Genuine clinical reasons for interruption (maternal instability, baby needing review) must not be counted as non-compliance → capture the documented reason
Staff habit of weighing the baby immediately is hard to change → involve maternity support workers, who usually do the weighing, in redesigning the checklist
Caesarean births may need a separate pathway (theatre staffing, recovery) → consider auditing vaginal and caesarean births separately
Improvement fading if the checklist reverts to the old order → update the printed and electronic checklist together
pearls: Involve an infant feeding lead/lactation consultant as co-investigator
Use UNICEF Baby Friendly Initiative standards as a familiar framework for staff
Display compliance alongside breastfeeding initiation rates, since the two are linked
Consider a champion on each shift to model early, uninterrupted skin-to-skin
Keep exclusions (resuscitation, neonatal unit admission) identical at re-audit

pitfalls: Vitamin K given but not documented, understating true practice → cross-check the drug administration record as well as the discharge checklist
Oral vitamin K needs multiple doses and a follow-up plan, which is often the part left undocumented → make follow-up plan a required sub-field, not just 'oral given'
Parents declining vitamin K may not have this decision recorded, only omission → make 'declined' an explicit selectable option, not a blank
Home births and midwifery-led unit births may use different documentation → include both settings in the sample
Improvement fading without a hard stop → build the field into the EPR rather than a paper checklist alone
pearls: Agree the exact wording of the three decision options with the neonatal team before cycle 1
Use a short scripted explanation for staff to give consistent information to parents
Cross-check a sample against the drug administration record to validate documentation accuracy
Involve postnatal ward staff, since some decisions are made after transfer from the birth room
Keep the same three decision categories at re-audit for comparability

pitfalls: Instrumental births at night or in an emergency may have prophylaxis forgotten → include an automatic EPR prompt rather than relying on memory
Penicillin allergy alternatives vary between trusts → confirm the local alternative with pharmacy before starting
Time from cord clamping (not from birth of baby) may be poorly documented → accept birth time as a proxy where clamping time is missing and note the limitation
Antibiotic prescribed but not actually administered within the window → check both prescribing and administration records
Fading compliance once the initial launch attention passes → include compliance in the routine maternity medicines dashboard
pearls: Involve the labour ward pharmacist in building the order set
Brief the on-call obstetric team as well as midwives, since doctors usually perform instrumental births
Use theatre/instrumental birth trolleys to physically prompt the antibiotic dose
Track reasons for non-administration (e.g. declined, allergy uncertainty) to target further work
Keep the same 6-hour window and instrument definitions at re-audit

pitfalls: Early transfer home or short postnatal stay can make the 72-hour window difficult → flag these babies for a home or GP-arranged NIPE and track separately
NIPE performed but recorded on paper not in the electronic system → check both records before counting as not done
Staffing gaps (no NIPE-trained practitioner on a shift) causing delay → escalate rota gaps to the neonatal/paediatric lead
Partial examinations (e.g. hips only) may be miscounted as complete → require all listed systems to be documented
Improvement fading after go-live → include NIPE completion in the daily safety huddle metrics
pearls: Recruit the NIPE lead practitioner as co-investigator
Use the existing electronic NIPE screening record as the primary data source to minimise extra work
Cross-check timing against discharge time to identify babies discharged before examination
Share compliance weekly with the postnatal ward as a visible metric
Keep the 72-hour definition and exclusions identical at re-audit

pitfalls: Mood assessment sometimes recorded narratively without a clear structure → agree a minimum structured question set (for example, the two Whooley questions) before cycle 1
Contacts done by phone may be less thoroughly documented than face-to-face → record contact type and compare compliance by type
Women lost to follow-up (moved, discharged early) reduce the denominator → record and report separately, not as non-compliance
Staff may feel this duplicates the perinatal mental health screening already done antenatally → explain this is about ongoing postnatal review, not booking screening
Improvement fading without a mandatory field → make the field compulsory in the EPR rather than an optional free-text box
pearls: Involve the perinatal mental health midwife lead as co-investigator
Use a validated brief tool (Whooley questions or Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale) consistently across the team
Feed back individual practitioner compliance sensitively alongside team-level results
Link this audit to the trust's perinatal mental health strategy and MBRRACE-UK maternal death recommendations
Keep the same assessment tool and contact definitions at re-audit

pitfalls: Meconium passage is often not asked about directly, only inferred from nappy charts → make it an explicit yes/no question at discharge
Early discharge before 24 hours makes assessment impossible at the point of discharge → record a safety-netting plan (what to look for, who to contact) for these babies instead
Staff may assume a normal-looking baby has passed meconium without checking → require a positive confirmation, not an assumption
Retrospective note review may miss verbal advice given without documentation → count only documented safety-netting as compliant
Improvement fading without a mandatory field → build it into the EPR discharge workflow
pearls: Combine this check with the existing discharge checklist review to avoid extra staff workload
Train maternity support workers, who often complete nappy/feeding charts, to flag meconium status
Use a simple laminated prompt card on the postnatal ward during the embedding phase
Share any missed or delayed diagnoses (anonymised) at induction/mandatory training to reinforce the rationale
Keep the same 24-hour definition and discharge timing categories at re-audit

pitfalls: Booking appointments are sometimes done by different staff groups (GP, community midwife) with different systems → confirm which system captures the assessment before cycle 1
Risk assessment done verbally but not documented → count only documented assessments as compliant
Missing risk factors (e.g. undocumented BMI or family history) can make the assessment incomplete even if a form was started → check completeness, not just presence of a form
Women booking late or via unbooked emergency attendance are hard to capture → report this group separately
Improvement fading if the mandatory field can be bypassed → confirm the EPR build genuinely blocks completion of booking without it
pearls: Involve the maternity thrombosis lead midwife/obstetrician as co-investigator
Use the RCOG/local VTE risk assessment tool your unit has already adopted, for consistency
Cross-check a sample of high-risk women to confirm the resulting thromboprophylaxis plan was actually carried out
Present findings alongside MBRRACE-UK data on VTE as a leading cause of direct maternal death, to support engagement
Keep the same risk assessment tool and definition of 'booking' at re-audit

pitfalls: Rectal examination may be performed but not documented → accept only documented examination as compliant; consider a spot-check with the woman's consent if under-recording is suspected
Junior staff may be uncomfortable performing or documenting a rectal examination → provide OASI care bundle training and supervision
Free-text notes may describe the tear without confirming a rectal examination was done → use a structured tick-box proforma rather than free text
Under-recognition of OASI, not just under-documentation, is the real risk → track third/fourth-degree tear detection rates alongside documentation compliance
Improvement fading without embedding in training → include the proforma in annual perineal repair skills updates
pearls: Base the audit on the national OASI care bundle project methodology so results are comparable with other units
Involve the OASI care bundle champion or perineal trauma lead as co-investigator
Use simulation training (perineal repair mannequins) to reinforce the systematic examination technique
Track OASI detection rate as a linked outcome measure alongside documentation compliance
Keep the same tear degree categories and examiner grade field at re-audit

pitfalls: Angle is difficult to measure precisely in a fast-moving birth → accept a disposable angle-guide indicator mark as a reasonable proxy for documentation
Only the mediolateral technique should be counted; midline episiotomy carries a higher OASI risk and should be flagged separately → record technique type explicitly
Junior obstetric and midwifery staff performing episiotomies may lack confidence with angle guides → provide simulation training before roll-out
Retrospective note review may only capture 'episiotomy performed' without angle detail → introduce the field prospectively for cycle 2
Improvement fading if angle guides run out of stock → confirm reliable procurement before wider roll-out
pearls: Use the same OASI care bundle framework and champion as the rectal-examination audit above, since they share a data collection visit
Pilot the angle guide with a small group of obstetricians and senior midwives first
Track OASI rate alongside angle-guide use as the outcome measure
Share results with the local perineal trauma multidisciplinary meeting
Keep the same technique and angle definitions at re-audit

pitfalls: RFM presentations are often managed hastily on a busy triage shift → make the proforma the fastest route, not an extra step, by pre-populating fields from the booking record
Recurrent RFM (which carries higher risk) may not be flagged if previous episodes are not cross-referenced → build a search of previous RFM presentations into the proforma
Growth chart review is sometimes skipped if a scan was 'recent' without checking the exact date → require the date of the last scan to be entered
Staff unfamiliar with the national checklist → provide short RFM update training before cycle 1
Improvement fading without an EPR-embedded proforma → build the checklist into the triage EPR template, not a paper insert
pearls: Base the audit directly on the NHS England SBLCB v3 checklist so it aligns with national reporting
Involve the maternity safety champion and RFM/stillbirth prevention lead as co-investigators
Track induction of labour and caesarean birth rates alongside compliance to watch for unintended over-intervention
Use anonymised MBRRACE-UK case summaries in training to explain the rationale
Keep the same first/recurrent RFM definitions at re-audit

pitfalls: Referral date and contact date are sometimes recorded in different systems → agree a single source of truth (the tobacco dependence service log) before cycle 1
Working days versus calendar days can be miscounted around weekends and bank holidays → define clearly and apply consistently
Women who decline contact should not be miscounted as a service delay → record 'declined contact' as a distinct outcome
Small tobacco dependence adviser team capacity may be the real bottleneck → report capacity alongside timeliness data to inform service planning
Improvement fading if referrals revert to a manual process → confirm the electronic referral route is the permanent default
pearls: Involve the tobacco dependence adviser team directly, since they hold the contact log
Benchmark local performance against the Maternity Services Dashboard smoking metrics
Track quit-date setting and 4-week quit rates alongside timeliness as a linked outcome
Present results at the local Smoking in Pregnancy Challenge Group network meeting for benchmarking
Keep the same working-day definitions at re-audit

pitfalls: Booking sometimes happens after 14 weeks, making the deadline unachievable for some women → report late bookers separately, not as non-compliance
Non-validated manual sphygmomanometers may still be in use in some clinic rooms → audit equipment as well as documentation
Risk assessment pathway/tool varies locally → confirm which tool (for example, a locally agreed algorithm per Appendix D of the care bundle) is in use before cycle 1
Community midwives booking women may use a different system from the hospital → include both settings in the sample
Improvement fading if old equipment is not fully withdrawn → remove non-validated monitors from clinical areas, not just add new ones
pearls: Involve the fetal growth surveillance/screening lead midwife as co-investigator
Audit equipment (monitor validation status) at the same time as the notes review
Use the care bundle's own process indicators for benchmarking against national data
Link with community midwifery teams early since much of this assessment happens outside hospital
Keep the same risk assessment pathway and 14-week deadline definition at re-audit

pitfalls: Bank, agency and locum staff are hardest to track and often missed by the trust's own training system → include a specific check for these staff groups at ward entry
Training completion recorded but competency assessment (a separate step) not done → audit both fields, not just attendance
Staff on leave (maternity, sickness) may appear overdue through no fault of their own → exclude or flag separately
Different training records systems for medical and midwifery staff can under- or double-count → reconcile both systems before reporting
Improvement fading without automatic alerts → confirm the alert system, not just a spreadsheet, is doing the tracking
pearls: Involve the practice development midwife/fetal monitoring lead and medical education lead as co-investigators
Use existing trust training system reports as the primary data source to avoid duplicate data entry
Report compliance by staff group so gaps (for example, obstetric trainees rotating in) are visible
Link training compliance data to the unit's Each Baby Counts and SBLCB v3 annual submission
Keep the same 12-month in-date definition at re-audit

pitfalls: Women with diabetes are a relatively small cohort per unit → extend the collection period to 3-6 months to reach an adequate sample
HbA1c may be requested but the result not reviewed or acted on → audit the surveillance plan, not just the blood test being done
Joint clinic records may be split between diabetes and obstetric systems → check both before concluding non-compliance
Definition of 'increased surveillance' varies between clinicians → agree a minimum data set (extra visit booked, dietitian/diabetes nurse referral, named consultant documented) before cycle 1
Improvement fading without an automatic order → build the 28-week HbA1c into the standard order set, not a manual reminder
pearls: Involve the joint diabetes antenatal clinic team (diabetes consultant, specialist nurse, dietitian) as co-investigators
Submit results to the National Pregnancy in Diabetes (NPID) audit for external benchmarking
Use the multidisciplinary joint clinic list as the sampling frame to minimise missed cases
Present findings against the unit's overall SBLCB v3 element 6 compliance
Keep the same 48 mmol/mol threshold and 28-week timing at re-audit

pitfalls: Very preterm births are relatively infrequent → extend the collection period to 6 months and use network-level data if the unit's numbers are too small
Temperature taken later than 1 hour may be recorded without the delay being obvious → record both the time and the value
Emergency preterm births may not allow time for the full normothermia bundle to be prepared → record whether the birth was planned or emergency and compare
Different thermometers/sites (axillary vs other) can give inconsistent readings → standardise the measurement method across the unit
Improvement fading without embedding → make the normothermia bundle a standing item on the preterm birth checklist, not a one-off initiative
pearls: Base the change directly on the BAPM normothermia toolkit for a ready-made implementation package
Involve neonatal nursing staff and the labour ward as joint owners, since both are responsible for temperature control
Benchmark against National Neonatal Audit Programme (NNAP) data
Link this audit to the wider perinatal optimisation pathway compliance metric in the care bundle
Keep the same gestation cut-off and timing definition at re-audit

pitfalls: Mothers recovering from caesarean birth or illness may be physically unable to express within 2 hours → record and report this separately from equipment or support failures
Milk expressed but not given to the baby promptly (e.g. delayed transport to neonatal unit) → capture both expressing time and administration time
Equipment availability (pumps, kits) at night or on a busy unit can be a genuine bottleneck → audit equipment availability alongside documentation
Small numbers of very preterm births → extend the collection period to 6 months
Improvement fading without embedding → make expressing support a standing item on the preterm admission checklist
pearls: Involve the infant feeding lead and neonatal nursing team as co-investigators
Use the BAPM maternal breast milk toolkit for a ready-made implementation package
Track necrotising enterocolitis and late-onset sepsis rates as linked longer-term outcome measures
Ensure postnatal ward and neonatal unit protocols are aligned so support does not stop at transfer
Keep the same 24-hour and 2-hour definitions at re-audit

pitfalls: PlGF testing may not be available on-site out of hours → confirm laboratory turnaround and availability before setting the target
Clinicians unfamiliar with the test or its interpretation may default to not requesting it → provide a short interpretation guide alongside the order set
Cost or sample-handling requirements may cause under-use → involve the laboratory in planning capacity
Borderline gestations (just under 20 or over 36+6 weeks) can cause miscounting → apply the window strictly and record exact gestation
Improvement fading without an order-set default → embed the test as an automatic tick rather than a manual add-on
pearls: Involve the maternal medicine lead and laboratory point-of-care/biochemistry lead as co-investigators
Use the existing NICE diagnostics guidance on PlGF-based testing as supporting evidence for clinicians
Track time to discharge or admission decision as a linked outcome measure
Present early results to reassure staff about turnaround time before wider roll-out
Keep the same gestation window and definition of 'suspected pre-eclampsia' at re-audit

pitfalls: Blood pressure can genuinely take days to settle after pre-eclampsia → discharge with a documented plan is an acceptable pass, not only an achieved target
Postnatal ward staff may not code pre-eclampsia consistently, making case-finding difficult → cross-check against the obstetric discharge summary and drug chart for antihypertensives
Early discharge (common practice) may mean the last reading in hospital is not representative → record whether community follow-up BP was also documented
Methyldopa should be changed to an alternative postnatally, which is a separate existing audit [NNA-194]; keep this audit focused on the BP target, not drug choice
Improvement fading without a mandatory field → build the check into the EPR discharge workflow
pearls: Involve the maternal medicine lead and postnatal ward matron as co-investigators
Cross-reference with the existing methyldopa-stopping audit [NNA-194] since both relate to postnatal hypertension management
Track readmission for hypertension/eclampsia as a linked outcome measure
Ensure community midwives and GPs receive a clear follow-up BP plan in the discharge letter
Keep the same 140/90 mmHg threshold at re-audit

pitfalls: Women may express a preference for a quicker resolution, making 'not chosen' common even when correctly offered → audit whether it was offered, not just whether it was chosen
Documented exceptions (haemorrhage risk, infection risk) must be captured accurately, not assumed → require the specific exception to be named
Staff turnover and locum medical staff may be unfamiliar with the first-line recommendation → include in early pregnancy unit induction
Verbal counselling without documentation understates true practice → use a structured, tick-box proforma
Fading compliance without embedding → make the counselling proforma the standard document for every miscarriage consultation
pearls: Involve the early pregnancy unit lead nurse/sonographer as co-investigator
Provide women with a written information leaflet alongside verbal counselling to support informed choice
Track re-attendance and unplanned admission rates for each management option as a linked outcome
Share results with GPs who often see women in the days after miscarriage diagnosis
Keep the same definition of 'confirmed miscarriage' and exceptions list at re-audit

pitfalls: Methotrexate for ectopic pregnancy is relatively uncommon per unit → extend the collection period to 12 months
Women may have blood tests done at their GP practice, with results not always returned promptly to the early pregnancy unit → include a system to actively chase GP-taken bloods
Non-attendance for follow-up bloods is a genuine risk in this population → record non-attendance separately and have an escalation plan for women who do not attend
hCG plateau/rise noted but reassessment not documented → audit the action taken, not just the blood test being done
Fading compliance without a recall system → use an active tracking list, not reliance on the woman remembering appointments
pearls: Involve the early pregnancy unit nurse/coordinator who typically manages this follow-up
Use a dedicated methotrexate follow-up tracker (spreadsheet or EPR task list) to actively chase results
Give women a clear written safety-netting leaflet on symptoms of rupture to watch for between visits
Review any case of treatment failure or rupture at the departmental morbidity meeting to close the loop
Keep the same follow-up schedule definition at re-audit

pitfalls: Some women decline an LNG-IUS due to a previous poor experience or personal preference → count 'offered but declined' as compliant, distinct from 'not offered'
Clinic letters may describe a treatment plan without stating what was discussed first → use a structured template rather than free text
Insertion capacity/waiting times for LNG-IUS fitting may discourage clinicians from offering it → review fitting clinic capacity alongside the audit
GP referral letters may already state a treatment preference that anchors the gynaecology consultation → record whether the referral influenced the discussion
Fading compliance without a template change → build the field into the standard clinic letter, not a separate audit form
pearls: Involve a gynaecology consultant with a special interest in HMB as co-investigator
Provide a patient decision aid on HMB treatment options to support shared decision-making
Track LNG-IUS fitting waiting times as a linked service measure
Share results with GPs to support earlier community offering of LNG-IUS where appropriate
Keep the same eligibility criteria at re-audit

pitfalls: Patients started on HRT by different prescribers (GP, menopause clinic, private) may fall outside a single system's recall → clarify which service owns follow-up before cycle 1
Reviews done opportunistically (e.g. at an unrelated appointment) may not be labelled as an 'HRT review' → search consultation content, not just appointment type
Patients who stop HRT themselves and do not attend should not be counted as a missed review by the service → record and exclude these appropriately
The audit needs a run-in period of over a year to capture both reviews, delaying results → consider an interim analysis of 3-month reviews only while waiting for 12-month data
Fading compliance without an automatic recall → build the recall into the electronic record's task system, not a manual diary
pearls: Involve the practice's menopause lead GP or specialist nurse as co-investigator
Use a search of the electronic prescribing record to build an accurate cohort of new HRT starts
Record side effects and reasons for stopping at review to feed into future prescribing discussions
Consider running this alongside a wider menopause care quality improvement project
Keep the same 3-month and 12-month definitions at re-audit

pitfalls: Compresses may be applied but not documented → add a simple tick box rather than relying on narrative notes
Equipment (compress warmers, single-use pads) may not be available in every room → audit equipment stocking alongside documentation
Precipitate births leave no time for a compress → record this as a distinct, acceptable exception
Staff unfamiliar with the 2023 update may not know this is now recommended → include in perineal care refresher training
Fading compliance if equipment runs out → add compress kits to the standard birth room stock list with a restocking check
pearls: Link this audit to the OASI care bundle programme and its existing champions
Trial the compress kit in one birth room before wider roll-out to solve practical issues
Track OASI rate over time alongside compress use as the outcome measure
Include the temperature-check step in training to ensure comfort and safety
Keep the same water-birth exclusion at re-audit

pitfalls: Hyperstimulation is relatively infrequent, making case-finding important → use an incident/CTG database search rather than relying on staff recall
Emergency documentation under pressure may be incomplete → use a dedicated proforma rather than free text
Ambiguity about what counts as 'removing where possible' for a slow-release pessary already largely absorbed → record what was physically done and any limiting factors
Tocolysis use is a 'consider' recommendation, not mandatory, so should not be scored as a hard fail → record as a separate, non-mandatory field
Fading compliance without a structured proforma → embed the proforma in the induction pathway documentation set
pearls: Cross-reference incident reports and CTG categorisation logs to find all episodes
Involve the labour ward risk midwife/obstetrician as co-investigator
Use simulation training to rehearse the hyperstimulation response as a team
Present findings alongside outcome (mode of birth, neonatal outcome) for context
Keep the same three-step definition at re-audit

pitfalls: Recognition time is often reconstructed retrospectively and may be imprecise → use the CTG trace timestamp as the primary source where available
This is a rare, high-stakes event, so numbers will be small → review every case rather than a sample, and extend the collection period as needed
Blame-focused review can suppress honest reporting → use a just-culture, learning-focused review process
Genuine clinical reasons for delay (for example, maternal resuscitation first) must be captured accurately → require a documented reason field, not just a pass/fail
Fading attention after an initial cluster of cases → keep this as a standing perinatal morbidity meeting agenda item
pearls: Review every case at the perinatal morbidity meeting rather than sampling, given the rarity and severity
Use simulation and "obstetric emergency" drills (crash caesarean, category 1) to rehearse the target interval
Link outcome data (cord gases, Apgar, NNU admission) to each case for full context
Feed learning into the unit's Each Baby Counts and MBRRACE-UK action plans
Keep the same definition of 'recognition time' and the 9-minute target at re-audit

pitfalls: High-risk factors may not be consistently identified or coded at booking → audit booking risk-factor recognition as well as the downstream pathway
Clinic capacity constraints may limit scan frequency regardless of intent → report capacity alongside compliance
Women who move between services (community/tertiary) may have incomplete records in one place → check both if the woman was referred onward
Missed scans due to non-attendance should be recorded separately from scans not offered → capture both
Improvement fading without automation → use an automatic referral trigger rather than relying on staff to remember
pearls: Involve the preterm birth prevention clinic lead as co-investigator
Use the SBLCB v3 Appendix F risk assessment and management algorithm as the reference standard
Track preterm birth rate in this cohort over time as a linked outcome measure
Coordinate with community midwives who identify risk factors at booking
Keep the same risk factor list and scanning interval definitions at re-audit

pitfalls: CGM funding/access pathways vary and may cause delay unrelated to clinical practice → record whether the delay was clinical or logistic (funding, device supply)
Small numbers of type 1 diabetes pregnancies per unit → extend the audit period to 12 months
Education/support may be provided by diabetes specialist nurses outside the joint clinic record → check both diabetes and obstetric records
Some women decline CGM for personal reasons, which is appropriate and should not be scored as non-compliance → record 'offered and declined' as compliant with the offer
Fading compliance without a mandatory field → build the field into the joint clinic booking proforma
pearls: Involve the diabetes specialist nurse and joint antenatal diabetes clinic lead as co-investigators
Use the NPID audit's own data fields to align local and national reporting
Track glycaemic control (time in range) as a linked outcome measure where CGM is accepted
Ensure equitable access regardless of postcode or funding pathway complexity
Keep the same definitions of 'offered' and 'already in use' at re-audit

pitfalls: Ectopic pregnancy volumes are relatively low per unit → extend the collection period to 12 months
hCG result timing relative to the decision may be unclear in retrospective notes → record the hCG date and value explicitly
Women may be judged clinically stable without this being explicitly documented → require an explicit statement, not an assumption
Follow-up non-attendance is itself a safety risk requiring an escalation plan → record any non-attendance and the service's response
Fading compliance without a structured proforma → embed the eligibility fields into the decision record, not a separate audit form
pearls: Involve the early pregnancy unit lead as co-investigator
Use a dedicated ectopic pregnancy tracking log to actively follow up all expectantly managed women
Review any case of rupture or emergency surgery after expectant management at the morbidity meeting to close the loop
Give women a clear written safety-netting leaflet on symptoms of rupture
Keep the same hCG thresholds at re-audit
